title: When demand outruns capacity: rate limits, retries, and backpressure
description: When requests arrive faster than a system can handle them, it either sheds the extra load or falls over. This quiz covers the limiter algorithms (token and leaky buckets, fixed and sliding windows), where to apply a limit (per IP, per user, or in the browser with debounce and throttle), how to tell clients to slow down (`429`, `Retry-After`, backoff with jitter), and how Node.js streams push back on a fast producer so a slow consumer doesn't run out of memory.

questions.title: Token bucket or leaky bucket: which one lets traffic burst?
questions.description: Both algorithms cap the long-run average rate. They treat short bursts differently.

images.alt: Two buckets side by side. The token bucket holds twenty tokens, refills at five per second, and spends one token per request. A full bucket admits twenty requests at once, and after that the five-per-second refill is the cap. The leaky bucket takes bursty input into a queue with a steady drain, so it absorbs bursts instead of passing them on, and drops overflow past its capacity. A closing note says the token bucket meters what may enter and the leaky bucket meters what may leave.
images.caption: Bursts pass on the left. A steady drain on the right.

options.text: The **token bucket** lets traffic burst up to its capacity, then settles to the refill rate. The **leaky bucket** drains at a fixed rate and smooths bursts away
The **leaky bucket** lets traffic burst up to its capacity. The **token bucket** forces a perfectly constant output rate
Both shape output into a perfectly constant rate and allow no bursts
Both allow unlimited bursts as long as the long-run average stays under the limit

questions.explanation:
A **token bucket** gains tokens at a fixed refill rate, up to a maximum called its *capacity*. Each request spends one token and goes through right away if a token is available. After an idle stretch the bucket is full, so a client can send a burst as large as the capacity. Only then does the limiter hold it to the refill rate. Think of it as saving up and then spending in one go.

A **leaky bucket** is a bucket with a hole in it. Requests pour in, and overflow when it's full, but they leave at a constant rate. The output stays smooth however bursty the input is.

So the token bucket tolerates bursts and the leaky bucket removes them. The other options either swap the two or claim they behave the same, which are the usual mix-ups. Some texts describe a *leaky bucket as a meter* that behaves like a token bucket. This question uses the more common *leaky bucket as a queue*.
questions.references: [Stripe: Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters) · [Wikipedia: Token bucket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Token_bucket)

questions.title: How many requests get through in the first instant of the burst?
questions.description: A token bucket holds at most **20** tokens and refills at **5** tokens per second. Each request costs 1 token. The bucket has been idle long enough to fill up, and then a client sends many requests at once.

images.alt: Two buckets side by side. The token bucket holds twenty tokens, refills at five per second, and spends one token per request. A full bucket admits twenty requests at once, and after that the five-per-second refill is the cap. The leaky bucket takes bursty input into a queue with a steady drain, so it absorbs bursts instead of passing them on, and drops overflow past its capacity. A closing note says the token bucket meters what may enter and the leaky bucket meters what may leave.
images.caption: Twenty tokens in the bucket, one spent per request.

questions.explanation:
The bucket's capacity is the largest burst it allows. While idle, it gains 5 tokens a second but stops at 20. An instantaneous burst takes no time, so the refill adds nothing, and the client can spend all 20 tokens at once. **20** requests go through.

The 21st request has to wait for a new token. From then on the client gets the sustained rate of 5 tokens a second, or one request every 200 ms. That's the whole design: capacity sets the burst size, and the refill rate sets the steady throughput. A leaky bucket with the same 5/s average would not allow this burst. It would release 5 requests a second from the start.

questions.title: What does the fixed-window limiter do with these 200 requests?
questions.description: A fixed-window limiter allows **100 requests per minute**, counted per clock minute (the counter resets at `:00`). A client sends 100 requests at `12:00:59.9` and another 100 at `12:01:00.1`.

images.alt: Two window schemes at a limit of 100 requests per minute. Under a fixed window, one batch of 100 sits at the end of the 12:00 window and another at the start of the 12:01 window, so about 200 requests are admitted in about a second. Under a sliding-window counter, a previous window of 80 requests and a current window of 20 are read through a trailing 60-second frame drawn 15 seconds into the current window, giving estimate = 20 + 80 × (60 − 15) / 60 = 80. Two cards compare the log, which stores one timestamp per request and is exact at O(n) per key, with the counter, which stores two integers per key and is approximate at O(1).
images.caption: Two legal batches, a fraction of a second apart, on either side of the reset.

options.text: All 200 get through within about a second, roughly twice the intended rate, because the batches land on either side of the window edge
All 200 are rejected, because the limiter adds them up to 200 for the minute
The second batch is automatically deferred to the `12:02` window
Only 100 get through in total, because fixed windows track a rolling 60-second total

questions.explanation:
A fixed window counts against the clock. At `12:00:59.9` the `12:00` window still has room, so the first 100 requests pass. A fifth of a second later the clock reaches `12:01`, the counter **resets to 0**, and the next 100 pass too. That's about 200 requests in one second, double the limit, even though each minute on its own counted only 100.

This boundary burst is the main weakness of fixed windows. Sliding-window algorithms fix it by measuring a window that ends at the current request instead of snapping to the clock. The wrong options describe sliding windows or queueing, which a fixed window doesn't do.
questions.references: [Cloudflare: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

questions.title: What is the estimated request count for the last 60 seconds?
questions.description:
A sliding-window *counter* uses 60-second windows. You are **15 seconds** into the current window. The **previous** window saw **80** requests, and the **current** window has **20** so far.

Use the standard weighted estimate `estimate = current + previous × (window − elapsed) / window` and round to the nearest whole request.

images.alt: Two window schemes at a limit of 100 requests per minute. Under a fixed window, one batch of 100 sits at the end of the 12:00 window and another at the start of the 12:01 window, so about 200 requests are admitted in about a second. Under a sliding-window counter, a previous window of 80 requests and a current window of 20 are read through a trailing 60-second frame drawn 15 seconds into the current window, giving estimate = 20 + 80 × (60 − 15) / 60 = 80. Two cards compare the log, which stores one timestamp per request and is exact at O(n) per key, with the counter, which stores two integers per key and is approximate at O(1).
images.caption: The last 60 seconds cover 45 s of the previous window and 15 s of this one.

questions.explanation:
The weight on the previous window is `(60 − 15) / 60 = 0.75`, so the estimate is `20 + 80 × 0.75 = 20 + 60 =` **80**.

An exact sliding window would count every request in the last 60 seconds, which needs a timestamp for each one. The counter assumes the previous window's requests were spread evenly. It keeps the share that still falls inside the last 60 seconds (45 of 60 seconds, or 75%) and adds everything from the current window. With a limit of 100, this request is allowed because 80 < 100. If the previous window had held 110, the estimate would be `20 + 110 × 0.75 = 102.5`, and the request would be blocked even though the current window alone is well under 100. In exchange for the approximation, the counter needs only **O(1) memory per key** (two integers) instead of the exact log's O(n).
questions.references: [Cloudflare: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

questions.title: How does a sliding-window log differ from a sliding-window counter?
questions.description: You need to keep limiter state for tens of millions of API keys in Redis, and you're choosing between two sliding-window implementations.

images.alt: Two window schemes at a limit of 100 requests per minute. Under a fixed window, one batch of 100 sits at the end of the 12:00 window and another at the start of the 12:01 window, so about 200 requests are admitted in about a second. Under a sliding-window counter, a previous window of 80 requests and a current window of 20 are read through a trailing 60-second frame drawn 15 seconds into the current window, giving estimate = 20 + 80 × (60 − 15) / 60 = 80. Two cards compare the log, which stores one timestamp per request and is exact at O(n) per key, with the counter, which stores two integers per key and is approximate at O(1).
images.caption: One timestamp per request, or two integers per key.

options.text: The **log** stores a timestamp for every request, so it's exact but uses O(n) memory per key. The **counter** keeps two integers per key, so it uses O(1) memory but only approximates
The **counter** is exact, and the **log** is an approximation that drifts over time
Both store one timestamp per request and differ only in how they evict old entries
The **log** uses constant memory, and the **counter** grows with the request rate

questions.explanation:
A sliding-window **log** keeps a timestamp for every request, for example in a Redis sorted set. It counts the entries newer than `now − window` and trims the rest. The count is exact, but memory and trimming cost grow with the number of requests in the window. That's **O(n) per key**, which adds up fast across tens of millions of keys.

A sliding-window **counter** keeps only the totals for the current and previous fixed windows, two integers, and combines them with the weighted estimate from the previous question. It needs **O(1) memory** and one calculation, but it's an approximation because it assumes the previous window's traffic was even. At this scale the memory savings win. Use the log only when you need an exact count. The wrong options swap which structure is exact and which uses constant memory.
questions.references: [Cloudflare: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

questions.title: What's the trade-off between per-IP and per-user rate limiting?
questions.description: You're deciding what to key a limiter on: the source IP, or the signed-in user or API key.

options.text: A per-IP limit can throttle many different users who share one address (an office NAT, carrier-grade NAT, a VPN exit). A per-user limit is fairer but has to know who the caller is, so it can't cover anonymous traffic
Per-IP is always fairer, because every user has their own IP address
Per-user limiting needs no authentication and works the same for anonymous and signed-in callers
Per-IP limiting stops abuse completely, because attackers can't change their source IP

questions.explanation:
The key decides who shares a bucket. Per-IP limits are cheap and work for anonymous traffic. But many unrelated people often share one public IP: everyone behind an office or campus NAT, mobile users behind carrier-grade NAT, or everyone on the same VPN exit. One heavy user, or one abuser, can use up the limit for all of them.

Keying on the user or API key gives each account its own budget wherever it connects from. That's fairer and more precise, but you have to know who the caller is, so it doesn't help before sign-in. Neither approach stops abuse on its own, since attackers rotate through botnets and proxy pools. Most production systems **use both**: a coarse per-IP limit at the edge for anonymous traffic, and a per-key limit for signed-in quotas.

questions.title: 429 or 503: which one says "it's you" and which says "it's me"?
questions.description: A gateway has to reject traffic in two situations: (a) one client went over its own per-key quota, and (b) the whole upstream is overloaded and shedding load for everyone.

images.alt: Five backoff steps for a base of 100 ms with no jitter: attempt 0 at 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800, and attempt 4 highlighted at 1600 ms. Below are two lanes. Without jitter, every client's retry lands on the same instant, labeled thundering herd. With jitter, the same retries spread across the interval. Two cards separate 429 Too Many Requests, meaning this client is over its own quota, from 503 Service Unavailable, meaning the upstream is shedding load for everyone. A note says Retry-After accepts only delay-seconds or an HTTP-date.
images.caption: It's you, or it's me.

options.text: (a) gets `429 Too Many Requests` because this client is over its limit, and (b) gets `503 Service Unavailable` because the server can't cope right now. Both can include `Retry-After`
(a) gets `503 Service Unavailable` and (b) gets `429 Too Many Requests`
Both should return `403 Forbidden`, since the request is refused either way
Both should return `200 OK` with an error body, so clients don't treat it as a failure

questions.explanation:
`429 Too Many Requests` (RFC 6585 §4) means *this client* sent too many requests in a given time, so the caller is at fault. `503 Service Unavailable` (RFC 9110 §15.6.4) means *the server* can't handle the request right now, because it's overloaded, deploying, or shedding load for everyone. Both can carry **`Retry-After`** to tell the client when to try again.

`403 Forbidden` is an authorization decision. It means "you can't do this," not "slow down," so retrying the same request is pointless. Returning errors as `200 OK` hides the failure from every proxy, cache, retry library, and dashboard that looks at the status code. Let the status code say what kind of failure it is, and let `Retry-After` say when to retry.

questions.title: Which are valid `Retry-After` values?
questions.description: RFC 9110 §10.2.3 says the value of `Retry-After` is **either** an HTTP-date **or** a non-negative number of seconds. Select **all** the values a server that follows the spec may send.

images.alt: Five backoff steps for a base of 100 ms with no jitter: attempt 0 at 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800, and attempt 4 highlighted at 1600 ms. Below are two lanes. Without jitter, every client's retry lands on the same instant, labeled thundering herd. With jitter, the same retries spread across the interval. Two cards separate 429 Too Many Requests, meaning this client is over its own quota, from 503 Service Unavailable, meaning the upstream is shedding load for everyone. A note says Retry-After accepts only delay-seconds or an HTTP-date.
images.caption: Two forms, and only two.

options.text: `Retry-After: 120`, meaning wait 120 seconds (delay-seconds)
`Retry-After: Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT`, an absolute HTTP-date
`Retry-After: 2m0s`, a Go-style duration string
`Retry-After: now+30`, a relative expression

questions.explanation:
RFC 9110 defines `Retry-After = HTTP-date / delay-seconds`. A plain non-negative integer such as `120` (wait 120 seconds) is valid, and so is a date in IMF-fixdate format such as `Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT`.

Duration formats from programming languages, or made-up ones, are not valid. `2m0s` is Go's `time.Duration` format, and `now+30` isn't defined anywhere. HTTP defines neither, so clients don't have to parse them and will usually ignore the header and fall back to their own backoff. When you send `Retry-After`, use whole seconds or a correctly formatted HTTP-date.

questions.title: How many milliseconds does the client wait before the retry at `attempt = 4`?
questions.description: A client retries on `429` with exponential backoff and **no** jitter: `delay = base × 2^attempt`, with `base = 100` ms. `attempt` is `0` for the first retry. The server keeps returning `429`.

images.alt: Five backoff steps for a base of 100 ms with no jitter: attempt 0 at 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800, and attempt 4 highlighted at 1600 ms. Below are two lanes. Without jitter, every client's retry lands on the same instant, labeled thundering herd. With jitter, the same retries spread across the interval. Two cards separate 429 Too Many Requests, meaning this client is over its own quota, from 503 Service Unavailable, meaning the upstream is shedding load for everyone. A note says Retry-After accepts only delay-seconds or an HTTP-date.
images.caption: The fifth step: `100 × 2⁴`.

questions.explanation:
`delay = 100 × 2^4 = 100 × 16 =` **1600** ms.

Attempts 0 through 4 wait `100, 200, 400, 800, 1600` ms. Each retry waits twice as long as the one before, so the client backs off quickly while the failures continue. In production you'd add two things:

- a **cap**, `min(cap, base × 2^attempt)`, so the delay can't grow forever
- **jitter**, a random delay within `[0, delay]`, so clients don't all retry at the same moment

AWS's "full jitter" formula combines both: `sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt))`.

questions.title: Which statements about adding jitter to backoff are true?
questions.description: After a spike of `429` and `503` responses, thousands of clients retry with exponential backoff. Adding *jitter* makes each client's delay random. Select **all** that apply.

images.alt: Five backoff steps for a base of 100 ms with no jitter: attempt 0 at 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800, and attempt 4 highlighted at 1600 ms. Below are two lanes. Without jitter, every client's retry lands on the same instant, labeled thundering herd. With jitter, the same retries spread across the interval. Two cards separate 429 Too Many Requests, meaning this client is over its own quota, from 503 Service Unavailable, meaning the upstream is shedding load for everyone. A note says Retry-After accepts only delay-seconds or an HTTP-date.
images.caption: Both lanes carry the same number of retries, spread differently.

options.text: Clients stop retrying at the same instant, so they don't overload the recovering server all over again (the "thundering herd")
The retries spread out over an interval, so the server faces a smaller spike
Every client is guaranteed a shorter wait than with plain exponential backoff
Every client follows the same predictable retry schedule, which is easier to reason about

questions.explanation:
Without jitter, clients that failed at the same moment compute the same backoff (2 s, then 4 s, then 8 s) and retry in waves. Each wave hits the server just as it's trying to recover. Jitter makes each delay random, for example with AWS's "full jitter": `sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt))`. The retries then arrive spread across the interval, with fewer collisions and a lower peak.

Jitter doesn't shorten any single client's wait. On a given roll, a client may wait longer. It also makes schedules random on purpose, since that randomness is what spreads the retries out. The goal is a lower peak load on the server, not lower latency for each client.

questions.title: What's the two-word name for this retry problem?
questions.description: Many clients fail at the same moment, all wait the *same* fixed backoff, and then retry together. The wave knocks the server over again just as it recovers, and the cycle repeats. Jitter is the usual fix.

images.alt: Five backoff steps for a base of 100 ms with no jitter: attempt 0 at 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800, and attempt 4 highlighted at 1600 ms. Below are two lanes. Without jitter, every client's retry lands on the same instant, labeled thundering herd. With jitter, the same retries spread across the interval. Two cards separate 429 Too Many Requests, meaning this client is over its own quota, from 503 Service Unavailable, meaning the upstream is shedding load for everyone. A note says Retry-After accepts only delay-seconds or an HTTP-date.
images.caption: The spike in the top lane is the herd.

questions.explanation:
It's the **thundering herd** problem. A large group of clients, processes, or threads all wake up or retry at the same moment and hit a shared resource together, so the server falls over again before it can recover. Fixed-delay retries cause it because every client calculates the same retry time.

The fix is to spread the herd out with **jitter** (a random backoff within `[0, delay]`), on top of exponential backoff and a cap. The term also shows up in operating systems, when one event wakes many threads that then fight over a lock. Caching has a close relative called a *cache stampede*: a popular key expires and every request goes to the origin at once.

questions.title: What does it mean when `writable.write()` returns `false`?

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable created by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response, with the writable's internal queue drawn between them as a fill bar against a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. When the queue is at or above the mark, write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still accepted and queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). When the queue drains below the mark, the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring the false only queues more chunks in memory until RSS kills the process, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: `false` means the queue is above the mark. The chunk was still accepted.

options.text: The internal buffer has reached `highWaterMark`. The chunk was still accepted and queued, but you should wait for the `'drain'` event before writing more
The write failed, the chunk was dropped, and you have to send it again
The chunk was bigger than `highWaterMark` and was rejected, so you should split it into smaller pieces
The stream has already ended, so you can't write to it anymore

questions.title: What happens when the source is much faster than the slow socket?

images.alt: A pipe from a Readable created by createReadStream to a slow Writable HTTP response, with the writable's internal queue drawn between them as a fill bar against a dashed highWaterMark line. Two panels follow. When the queue is at or above the mark, write(chunk) returns false, the chunk is still accepted and queued, and pipe() calls readable.pause(). When the queue drains below the mark, the 'drain' event fires and pipe() calls readable.resume(). A closing note says that ignoring the false only queues more chunks in memory until RSS kills the process, so backpressure protects memory rather than the socket or the disk. It also says objectMode counts objects, so the default mark is 16 objects instead of 16 KB.
images.caption: Nothing pauses the source, so the queue in the middle keeps growing.

options.text: Node keeps accepting chunks and buffering the ones it hasn't sent yet. The buffer grows until the process runs out of memory and crashes
`write()` blocks the event loop until each chunk is sent, so memory stays flat but throughput drops
Node notices the imbalance and pauses the source for you
Chunks past `highWaterMark` are quietly thrown away, so memory stays safe

questions.explanation:
`highWaterMark` is a hint, not a hard limit. If you ignore `false` from `write()` and keep writing, Node doesn't block and doesn't drop data. It queues every chunk in the writable's internal buffer, and the buffer keeps growing because the producer is faster than the consumer. Memory climbs until the process is killed for running out of it, which is exactly what backpressure is meant to prevent.

The other options are common myths. `write()` doesn't block: it returns right away, so it can't slow anything down by stalling the event loop. Node doesn't pause a source you drive by hand. Only `pipe()` and `pipeline()` do that. And chunks past the mark are buffered, never dropped. Wait for `'drain'` yourself, or better, use `stream.pipeline(fastSource, slowSocket, cb)`, which handles backpressure, errors, and cleanup for the whole chain.

questions.title: Why is a bounded queue better than an unbounded one under overload?
questions.description: A service gets work faster than it can process it, for a long stretch. One design puts everything in an **unbounded** in-memory queue. The other uses a **bounded** queue and rejects (sheds) new work once it's full.

options.text: With an unbounded queue, latency and memory keep growing until the process runs out of memory, and callers often time out before their old items run. A bounded queue with load shedding rejects quickly (for example with `429` or `503`) and keeps the system responsive
The unbounded queue is safe because, by Little's Law, a longer queue raises throughput above the service rate
The bounded queue is worse, because rejecting requests always lowers goodput compared with serving them all eventually
Queue length doesn't affect latency as long as the average arrival rate equals the average service rate

questions.explanation:
The **service rate** μ limits throughput, and a bigger queue doesn't add any processing power. If arrivals λ stay above μ, the backlog grows by about `(λ − μ)` items a second with no end. **Little's Law** (`L = λ × W`) shows what that means: the more items waiting (L), the longer each one waits (W). An unbounded queue turns overload into ever-growing latency. Requests wait so long that clients time out, and the server spends its capacity on responses nobody is waiting for. Memory grows too, until the process is killed.

**Load shedding** fixes this. Cap the queue and reject the overflow right away with a `429` or `503` and `Retry-After`. The work you accept stays fresh, and the server stays up. The last option skips a detail: even when λ matches μ on average, bursts make the queue and latency swing, and queueing delay rises sharply as utilization gets close to 100%.

questions.title: Which behavior is debounce, and which is throttle?
questions.description: Two browser techniques for noisy events like keystrokes, scroll, and resize. One fires once *after* the activity stops. The other fires at most once per interval *while* the activity continues.

options.text: **Debounce** waits for a pause and then fires once, which suits search-as-you-type. **Throttle** fires at most once per interval during continuous events, which suits scroll and resize handlers
**Throttle** fires once after the activity stops, and **debounce** fires at a steady pace during it
Both fire on every event but delay each callback by a fixed amount
They're two names for the same timer technique

questions.explanation:
Both turn a flood of events into fewer calls, with different timing. **Debounce** restarts a timer on every event and fires only when the events stop for the chosen interval. Fifty keystrokes in a row trigger one call, after the user pauses. Use it for search-as-you-type or for work that should run once a resize is finished.

**Throttle** sets a steady ceiling of one call per interval while events keep coming. A scroll that fires hundreds of events a second becomes, say, one handler call every 100 ms. Debounce when you only care about the final state. Throttle when you want regular updates during the activity, just not too many. They're the browser-side version of server rate limiting: both protect something from being called too often, and these do it before a request is even sent.
